Mr. Nutting: The attitude of His Majesty's Government to the Schuman Plan was stated in a Declaration issued in Washington on 14th September by Mr. Acheson, Monsieur Schuman and my right hon. Friend's predecessor. The relevant passages of this Declaration were as follows: 8 "The Three Ministers recognise that the initiative taken by the French Government concerning the creation of a European coal and steel community and a European defence community is a major step towards European unity. They welcome the Schuman Plan as a means of strengthening the economy of Western Europe and look forward to its early realisation. … The Government of the United Kingdom desires to establish the closest possible association with the European Continental Community at all stages in its development." I am authorised by my right hon. Friend to reaffirm this Declaration on behalf of His Majesty's Government.
60. Mr. Black asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs whether he will arrange for United Nations stamps to be available for sale in this country for sterling.

Mr. Nutting: A letter has recently been received from the United Nations Postal Administration concerning arrangements for the sale of United Nations stamps for philatelic purposes. This letter is being considered, but meanwhile United Nations stamps will be on sale in Paris during the current session of the United Nations Assembly, and arrangements have been made for a limited number to be imported from France for sale by dealers in the United Kingdom.

61. Mr. Sorensen asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs who, at present, exercises responsibility for relief work in Korea; in addition to the £10 million contributed for this purpose by His Majesty's Government, how much is available; and how relief and reconstruction is now proceeding.

Mr. Nutting: The responsibility for relief work in Korea is at present held by the United Nations Civil Assistance Command. By far the largest contribution has been made by the United States Government through the Unified Command. Excluding what the United Kingdom and United States have contributed, the total of cash and commodities pledged or contributed from all other sources amounts to about $24 million.

Good progress has been made in relief work in that part of Korea under the control of the United Nations. Adequate food supplies have been made available to the Korean civil population and there have been no major epidemics; but it has not yet been possible to embark on any large-scale reconstruction of housing.
62. Mr. R. E. Winterbottom asked the Minister of National Insurance why persons in receipt of supplementary pensions were not given the full benefit of the recent increase in pensions.

Mr. Peake: As supplementary assistance is based on need, some reductions in assistance were inevitable as the result of the new rates of pension and assistance fixed in the summer. But over three-quarters of the pensioners concerned have received the full benefit of the new pension rates. Of the remainder, all except a small number have had their incomes increased.

64. Dr. Stross asked the Minister of National Insurance whether his attention has been drawn to the case of Mr. John Bryan of Stoke-on-Trent, who died recently as a result of silicosis following a lifetime's work as a china turner; and whether his dependants are to receive compensation for his death.
Mr. Peake: I understand that the hon. Member has in mind a possible claim to Workmen's Compensation. As he knows, such cases are decided by the ordinary courts and I have no power to intervene.

63. Mr. P. Roberts asked the Minister of National Insurance whether he will pay the full sickness benefit contribution to ex-Service pensioners irrespective of whether the pensioner is receiving other assistance, in view of the fact that the full contribution has been paid by the pensioner for the benefit of such sick pay.

Mr. Peake: Personal sickness benefit is normally payable in full to an ex-Service man with a war disability pension. 10 and 1 assume that my hon. Friend is referring to adjustments which may have to be made in some cases to prevent overlapping of increases for dependants under the different schemes. The National Insurance (Overlapping Benefits) Regulations, 1948, which govern the position, gave effect to recommendations made by the National Insurance Advisory Committee. I am sending a copy of the Committee's Report to my hon. Friend. I see no reason to differ from the Committee's conclusions.

65. Mr. Lewis asked the Minister of National Insurance if he will arrange to issue all old age pensioners with a free purchasing voucher, enabling them to buy one hundredweight of coal per week; and what is the estimated cost if limited to the winter period.
Mr. Peake: I have no power to make such arrangements. I regret that the information asked for in the second part of the Question is not available.
67. Mr. P. Roberts asked the Minister of Fuel and Power whether he will take immediate steps to safeguard the domestic consumer's ration of coal during the coming winter.
Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: I would refer the hon. and gallant Member to the statement I made to the House on 8th November.

68. Mr. H. Hynd asked the Minister of Fuel and Power if he is aware of the shortage of domestic fuel in Accrington and the fact that merchants are introducing an unofficial rationing system; and, in view of the special requirements of that area, whether he proposes to allocate additional supplies.

70. Mr. Awbery asked the Minister of Fuel and Power if he is aware of the shortage of domestic coal in Bristol; and what steps he proposes to take to meet effectively the demands of the householders during the coming winter.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: I would refer the hon. Members to the statement which I
11 made to the House on 8th November. As regards the incidence of the shortage as between one part of the country and another, there are established arrangements, which have stood the test of some years experience, for ensuring a fair distribution of available supplies.

69. Brigadier Medlicott asked the Minister of Fuel and Power what stocks of coal and coke for domestic use are now held in the Eastern Region; and how these stocks compare with the amounts held at the corresponding period a year ago.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: Stocks of house coal held in merchants' yards in the Eastern Region on 27th October last amounted to 83,000 tons, as compared with 167,000 tons at the corresponding date a year ago. For coke, the figures are 13,000 tons this year, as against 22,000 tons a year ago.

72. Major Anstruther-Gray asked the Minister of Fuel and Power how much coal and coke for domestic use is now held in the Scottish Region; and whether he is satisfied that these stocks are adequate for a normal winter.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: Merchants' stocks of house coal, coke and anthracite and boiler fuel in Scotland on 27th October amounted to 197,000 tons. This compares with 264,000 tons at the same time last year.
As regards the second part of the Question, I would refer to the statement which I made to the House on 8th November.

74. Mr. Renton asked the Minister of Fuel and Power whether he is aware that there is a shortage of coke in rural districts in Huntingdonshire and that this is a handicap to people who rely upon coke for cooking and for heating bath water; and what steps are being taken to overcome this shortage.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: There is not sufficient coke available to meet all demands, but I do not think that the shortage in the rural districts of Huntingdonshire has been any greater than in other parts of the country.
77.Mr. Rankin asked the Minister of Fuel and Power if, in the interests of conserving our resources of fuel and power, he is prepared to make arrangements to suspend mid-week sport.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: I understand that when this was reviewed last winter, there was no evidence that mid-week sport in general had any effect on the production of coal. The St. Leger was the exception to this rule, and the Stewards of the Jockey Club kindly consented to have the race run on a Saturday this September. I am, however, having the evidence examined again, and if necessary I will consult my right hon. Friends the Secretary of State for the Home Department and the Secretary of State for Scotland.
73. Mr. R. Robinson asked the Minister of Fuel and Power the present position of the experiment in the underground gasification of coal conducted under the auspices of his Department.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: The experimental work is being continued at Newman Spinney, near Sheffield, and preparations are being made to conduct experiments at Bayton, in Worcestershire, where it is expected that two coal seams will be ignited early in 1952. The seams and geological characteristics differ at the two sites, thus permitting the techniques to be tested in different conditions.
The experiments are on a relatively small scale, designed to discover the technical and economic facts necessary to determine whether a full-scale operation should be planned.
75. Mr. Anthony Greenwood asked the Minister of Fuel and Power when it is proposed to publish the Report of tile Working Panel on Supplies of Solid Smokeless Fuel.
Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: It is not proposed to publish the Interim Report of the Working Party to which the hon. Member refers.

76. Mr. Anthony Greenwood asked the Minister of Fuel and Power what plans he has for expanding the production of solid smokeless fuel; and what percentage increase in present production is anticipated during the next five years.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: Plans for expanding the production of solid smokeless fuel are primarily the responsibility of the National Coal Board and the Gas Council. But, as I said in the House on Thursday last, the supply of boiler fuel is below the demand, and I shall carefully watch the progress that is being made to increase the output of solid smokeless fuels generally.
I understand that the industries concerned are not yet in a position to make reliable forecasts of the increased production of smokeless fuels expected in the next five years.
79. Mr. Iain MacLeod asked the Attorney-General whether it is proposed to accept the recommendations of the Committee into the Law of Intestacy.
The Attorney-General: My noble Friend the Lord Chancellor has this question under consideration.

80. Commander Porsey asked the Attorney-General the number of cases affected by the postponement of the Hull Quarter Sessions on 8th October; the number of cases in court when the sessions were adjourned on 31st October; the number partly heard; and the number of cases whose remand in custody was extended because of the postponement and adjournment, respectively.

The Attorney-General: There were 20 cases affected by the postponement of the Hull Quarter Sessions on the 8th October; the number of cases remaining in the list when the Sessions were adjourned on 31st October was four, of which one was part-heard; the number of cases in which remand in custody was extended because of the postponement was 11 and because of the adjournment, four.

81. Mr. Edward Davies asked the Minister of Health what instructions or advice have been given to local authorities relating to the recent increase of 4s. per week to old age pensioners resident in hostels; and whether any part of the increase has actually reached the pensioners by way of pocket money.

Mr. Crookshank: The amount of pocket money that these pensioners may receive is governed by Statutory Regulations which do not authorise me to give instructions to local authorities in the matter. I have no record of the amounts of pocket money actually paid.

Miss Ward asked the Minister of Health if he will circulate in the OFFICIAL REPORT details of the schemes which have been postponed by the regional hospital boards as a result of the instructions issued prior to 25th October to cut their estimates on capital expenditure.
Mr. Crookshank: I regret that I have no detailed information on this point.
83. Sir I. Fraser asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether he can now indicate the form in which the Government will review the position of pensioners, including war pensioners.
Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: We are reviewing these important questions in the course of the Government's general review of expenditure.

Mr. H. Hynd asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer what was the amount of tax collected for the period January to September, 1951, inclusive, from the Pool Betting Duty imposed on greyhound racing totalisators.

Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: The amount of Pool Betting Duty collected in the period
15 January to September, 1951, in respect of greyhound racing totalisators was £5,137,838.
Mr. J. B. Hynd asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer when His Majesty's Government proposes to proceed with the abolition of the purchase tax.
Mr. R. A. Butler: In the circumstances explained to the House last week, I can see no early prospect of abolishing this tax. For the rest, I cannot anticipate Budget decisions.
84. Mr. Irving asked the Minister of Education if he will make free milk available to children over five years of age who are denied school accommodation.
Mr. Pickthorn: No. The powers of local education authorities do not enable them to include in the milk in schools scheme children who are not in attendance at school.

85. Mr. Awbery asked the Secretary of State for War if he is aware of the discontent among the civilian employees of the three Service Departments in Singapore and Malaya because of the delays in 16 dealing with wage claims; and what action he proposes to take in this matter.

Mr. Head: For many months the unions representing local non-industrial employees of the Service Departments in Singapore and Malaya have been pressing that local government rates of pay should be applied to employees of the Service Departments.

The pay policy adopted by the Service Departments has been to keep broadly in line with the level of total emoluments paid by the general body of local good employers, private as well as public, for similar work. This policy has recently been reaffirmed and the local commanders-in-chief have been instructed to inform the unions accordingly in reply to their representations.
The commanders-in-chief have power to review the pay and allowances of local employees at any time, and in conformity with the policy described many improvements have been made recently.
Mr. Grimond asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether the Government will amend the Town and Country Planning Act so as to abolish the development charge in rural areas.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I am not yet in a position to make any statement about possible amendments of this Act.

3. Mr. P. Roberts asked the Minister of Pensions whether he will consult the Minister of Health with a view to ensuring that ex-Service pensioners in need of medical treatment shall, if possible, be sent to Ministry of Pensions' hospitals rather than to the ordinary hospitals.

Mr. Amory: Ex-Service pensioners requiring treatment for their war disabilities are encouraged to enter Ministry of Pensions hospitals. Frequently, however, a pensioner, for personal reasons, prefers to enter a hospital nearer his home, and unless he is in need of very specialised treatment which cannot be provided in that hospital his wishes are met.

59. Mr. Peter Freeman asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether he will authorise a duly-elected official of an old age pensioners' association to countersign the certificate of application for tobacco-duty relief by a pensioner in addition to the other 15 categories already recognised.

Mr. R. A. Butler: The present list of categories, which has been in use since 1947, gives the pensioner a wide choice, and I should need clear evidence that it is seriously inadequate before I could feel justified in authorising the extra expense involved in revising the forms.

60. Mr. Peter Freeman asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer if he will now alter the present coinage system to allow for 10 pennies to a shilling and so take a preliminary step towards a decimal system.

Mr. R. A. Butler: No, the replacement of the existing bronze coinage by new coins of different value would involve an impossible burden on our present resources of material and labour. The alternative of increasing by 20 per cent. the value of the bronze coinage now in circulation is likewise unsatisfactory.

68. Mr. A. Lewis asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer if he will give an assurance that the Government will not cut any of the social services; and whether it is his intention to make financial provision for an increase in the old-age pension.

Mr. R. A. Butler: I would refer the hon. Member to the statement of the Government's intention in the Gracious Speech. The needs of old age pensioners are ever present in my mind, but I cannot make any statement.

69. Mr. Leslie Hale asked the Chancellor whether he is aware of the hardship caused by old age pensions being subject to Income Tax; and whether he will introduce amending regulations to remove this hardship.

Mr. R. A. Butler: An old age pensioner with no other income would be exempt from tax. Where there is other income, I do not think that old age pensions should be treated differently from other retirement pensions by being left out of account in computing total income.
71. Sir J. Lucas asked the Financial Secretary to the Treasury if he can now state the amount of reserves taken over when the Bank of England was nationalised.
Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: No.
72. Mr. Porter asked the Financial Secretary to the Treasury what is the estimated saving to his Department by the voluntary reduction of salary contemplated by certain Ministers.

Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: I would refer the hon. Member to the answer given today by my right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer to the hon. Members for Northampton (Mr. Paget), Blackburn, East (Mrs. Castle), Bristol, South-East (Mr. Benn), Swindon (Mr. T. Reid), and Sheffield. Park (Mr. Whiney).

73. Mr. Porter asked the Financial Secretary to the Treasury to what extent allowances are made in regard to Income Tax relief to Ministers and junior Ministers who opt to use their own cars in preference to those supplied from the official pool.

Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: Expenses in- curred by a Minister of the Crown in using his own car for travelling when an official car is available would not qualify for relief from Income Tax under Rule 9 of Schedule E, because the Minister would not be "necessarily obliged" to incur them.
Mr. Donnelly asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether he is prepared to consider any scheme for payment of post- war credits to persons who are chronically sick or disabled.

Mr. R. A. Butler: I would refer the hon. Member to the reply I gave today to the hon. Members for Itchen (Mr. Morley), Gateshead, East (Mr. Moody), Small Heath (Mr. F. Longden), Bradford. South (Mr. George Craddock). and Cardiff. West (Mr. G. Thomas).

75. Mr. Janner asked the President of the Board of Trade what is the present position with regard to the Committee of Copyright; what changes there have been in the composition of this committee since it was first appointed; whether it has yet completed the taking of evidence; and when its report is likely to be available.

Mr. H. Strauss: The Committee has just completed the taking of oral evidence in public, the first stage of its task. The Chairman of the Committee, my noble Friend the Marquess of Reading, has resigned on his appointment as Parlia- mentary Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, and Sir Henry Gregory, K.C.M.G., C.B., a member of the Com- mittee, has been appointed in his place. There have been no other changes in the Committee. The report of the Committee is not expected to be available for some months.

76. Mr. P. Roberts asked the President of the Board of Trade whether, until the international position is clarified, he will give instructions to hold up the fulfilment of the big orders from Persia for steel for railway purposes, which steel is vitally needed in other parts of the Commonwealth.

Mr. Hopkinson: The licences which had been given for the export to Persia of railway track equipment, including rails, sleepers and fastenings, were revoked on the 10th September and cargoes of these goods which were already en route to Persia were requisitioned. No further licences for the export of these goods to Persia are being issued for the present.
78. Mr. Chetwynd asked the President of the Board of Trade whether he will maintain the priority of the development areas with regard to factory construction.
80. Mr. Peart asked the President of the Board of Trade, what restrictions are to be placed on factory building in development areas.

Mr. Hopkinson: Authorisation for factory building in development areas will be subject to the general considerations put forward by my right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer on 7th November during the debate on the Address.
79. Mr. Erroll asked the President of the Board of Trade when he intends to restore the Liverpool Cotton Exchange.
Mr. H. Strauss: I would refer my hon. Friend to the statement made by my right hon. Friend on Friday last during the debate on the Address.
12. Mr. Gower asked the President of the Board of Trade when the Monopolies Commission's Report on Electric Lamps will be published; and if he will make a statement about the report.

Mr. P. Thorneycroft: The Report was. published today. The Commission have
21 found that conditions to which the Monopolies and Restrictive Practices (Inquiry and Control) Act, 1948, applies, prevail as respects the supply of electric lamps, since about 60 per cent. of both filament and discharge lamps are supplied by members of the Electric Lamp Manufacturers' Association who operate a number of arrangements which restrict competition in the industry.

The Report shows that the E.L.M.A. firms agree together on the types of lamps to be manufactured and on common manufacturers' prices for each type; they also lay down the prices to be charged at each stage of distribution and enforce these prices by collective sanctions. Besides the "stop-list" used for this purpose, there are also "exclusive dealing" arrangements requiring all wholesalers who sell E.L.M.A. lamps not to sell lamps made by other manufacturers; and retailers get better terms if they agree to confine themselves to E.L.M.A. lamps.

There are also "sales quota" arrangements by which a manufacturer in the E.L.M.A. group cannot increase his share of the total U.K. market (relative to other members of the group) without incurring penalties.

The Commission also describe in detail the patent policies followed by members of E.L.M.A., their attitude to standardisation and the position with regard to certain components which manufacturers outside the association obtain from E.L.M.A. members.

The report shows that outside the Electric Lamps Manufacturers Association there are a number of firms—known as the "controlled companies"—which are jointly owned by E.L.M.A. members and which market lamps through the chain stores, usually at lower prices than E.L.M.A. lamps.

The Commission note that the E.L.M.A. system is markedly less restrictive now than in 1939. The new patent policy proposed by the members of E.L.M.A. who own patents is more liberal and the "quota" arrangements and the arrangements about the sale of components to non-members have been made less rigorous. The Report also shows that prices and profits, which were unduly high before the war, are now—except in the case of motor lamps—on average, moderate.

The Commission see in the exchange of technical knowledge within the industry a considerable advantage to offset the potential dangers of the manufacturers' price-ring and they do not recommend that the fixing of common manufacturers' prices should be prohibited, provided that two conditions are fulfilled. The first condition is that the exchange of technical knowledge should extend to all manufacturers within the system of common prices; the second is that the prices should be reasonable. The Commission suggest that the Government should review them from time to time.

Moreover, the Commission recommend certain other safeguards and changes in the system, failing which they think that it may be expected to operate against the public interest in the future; and anything which had the effect of reducing the degree of competition advocated in these recommendations would make it necessary, in the view of the Commission, to reexamine the whole question. The principal recommendations under this head are as follows:
(a) E.L.M.A. members who supply components (apart from patented components and ready-coiled filaments), should make them equally available to members and non-members at prices which are not higher to non-members than to members.
(b) If the new patent policy proposed by E.L.M.A. members results in reducing the degree of competition to which E.L.M.A. firms are subjected, the whole question should be reexamined.
(c) E.L.M.A. members should give an assurance that the "controlled companies" will continue to provide a measure of competition by supplying cheap lamps, but will not be used as "fighting companies" against independent manufacturers.
(d) The sales quota arrangements should be brought to an end.
(e) On the distribution side, the collective enforcement of resale price maintenance and all the "exclusive dealing" arrangements and ancillary arrangements regarding rebates and other payments should be brought to an end.

One member of the Commission—Mrs. Joan Robinson—in an addendum to the
23 Report considers that it is unrealistic to expect the "controlled companies" to compete freely and effectively with E.L.M.A. members while still being owned by them and recommends that the Government should acquire the share capital of these companies. This would, in her view, generally strengthen the effect of the other recommendations.

84. Mr. Swingler asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether, in view of the housing shortage, he will increase the allocations of houses to the borough and rural district of Newcastle-under-Lyme.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I shall be willing to increase the allocation in accordance with progress made.

85. Mr. Alport asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government if his attention has been drawn to the successful experiment carried out by the Eastern Federation of Building Trades Employers at Ipswich in constructing houses at a low cost and with a high standard of amenity; and whether he will encourage the development of this experiment in the future.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I have not yet had an opportunity of studying the particular scheme, but I am certainly ready to encourage suitable proposals for building cheaper houses.

86. Mr. Alport asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government if he will take steps to ensure that those who are anxious and able to build houses for their own occupation with their own labour are given special facilities and encouragement to do so.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I am considering in what ways house ownership can most appropriately be encouraged.

87. Mr. H. Brooke asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government the number of new houses and flats under 24 construction in October, 1950, and October, 1951; and the total number completed, or estimated to be completed, in the years ending 30th September, 1951, and 30th September, 1952, respectively.

Mr. H. Macmillan: The numbers under construction on 1st October, 1950, and on 1st October, 1951, were 170,944 and 187,205 respectively. 168,026 were completed in the year ended 30th September, 1951. I cannot yet give a reliable estimate of the number likely to be completed during the succeeding year.

Mr. Chetwynd asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government how many permanent houses were completed at 25th October, 1951; how many were under construction; how many sites were prepared; and how many houses were approved.
Mr. H. Macmillan: The latest available figures are given in the Housing Return 30th September, 1951 (Cmd. 8389) obtainable from the Vote Office.

88. Mrs. Mann asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government the proportionate percentages of the housing target of 300,000 per annum, to be allocated to Scotland, England and Wales, respectively.
Mr. H. Macmillan: No, but I have no doubt that my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Scotland will strive to get his fair proportion.

89. Mr. Mulley asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government what steps he proposes to take to increase the number of houses to be built in Sheffield; and if he will increase the quota of local authority houses.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I am ready to increase the allocation in accordance with progress made.

90. Mr. Blenkinsop asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether he will now allow the continuation of the Newcastle County Borough Council's five-year scheme to enable the pre-war housing estates and other property to be supplied with electricity.
Mr. H. Macmillan: Work is proceeding on 773 houses, but I am informed that the North-Eastern Electricity Board are at present unable to do more owing to the limited resources available.

91. Mr. Blenkinsop asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether he will give an assurance that no additional charges will fall upon housing authorities following the increase in interest rates.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I cannot add to my right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer's statement until the results of the subsidy review are laid before the House.

93. Mrs. Mann asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government if, in view of the shortage of building materials, he will give an assurance that present housing standards will be continued, particularly in relation to the space area of each house.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I would refer the hon. Member to the reply I gave on 9th November to the hon. Member for Dartford (Mr. N. Dodds).

94. Dr. King asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether he will consider the re-introduction of grants from the Treasury to give rate aid to war-damaged towns such as Southampton, which will still suffer extra local financial burdens because of their losses during the war.
Mr. H. Macmillan: My predecessors did not feel warranted in extending these grants after March of this year and I cannot see my way to reverse their decision.

95. Mr. R. D. Williams asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government if, in view of the impending reductions in the capital investment programme, he will give an assurance that special consideration will be given to the needs of bomb-damaged cities, such as Exeter.

96. Mr. J. J. Astor asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government what 26 effect the building restrictions will have on reconstruction in war-damaged cities in general and Plymouth in particular.

97. Mr. Elwyn Jones asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether His Majesty's Government will give priority in re-housing to bomb-damaged areas like West Ham, where the housing needs are greatest; and what steps are to be taken to ensure that they receive such priority.

99. Mr. A. Lewis asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether he will give an assurance that bomb-damaged towns and cities will receive a special priority allocation out of the 300,000 houses per annum.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I am aware of the needs of the war-damaged cities, and I will give them as sympathetic consideration as I can.
104. Mr. H. Brooke asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government how many new houses and flats have so far been completed under the provisions of the New Towns Act, 1946.
Mr. H. Macmillan: On 31st October, 1951, 2,362 new dwellings had been completed by Development Corporations in the new towns in England and Wales.

98. Mr. Elwyn Jones asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government what action His Majesty's Government proposes to take, in view of the recent decision of the Divisional Court in the King v. Folkestone Rent Tribunal,ex parte Sharkey, to enable rent tribunals to grant security of tenure to tenants who have failed or have been unable to refer their tenancies to the rent tribunal before the service of a notice to quit upon them by their landlords.
Mr. H. Macmillan: None.

102. Mr. Lindgren asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government how many local authorities in England and Wales have, since 1945, made advances under the Small Dwellings Acquisition Acts and the Housing Acts to enable people to buy their own houses; how much has been advanced; and for how many houses.
Mr. H. Macmillan: The number of authorities is 921, including 19 county councils; the amount advanced up to 31st March, 1951, is £40,078,174 for 47,806 houses.
Mr. Dodds asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government if he will make a statement on the prospects for increased supplies of timber, cement and bricks for an extended housing programme.
Mr. H. Macmillan: It is too early yet for any precise statement.

103. Mr. Renton asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether he is aware that local authorities are uncertain as to whether or not it is in order for them when laying new water mains to provide connections from them to the boundaries of properties free of charge; and what steps he will take to clarify the matter.
Mr. H. Macmillan: A circular was sent recently to local authorities to clear up this point. I am sending my hon. Friend a copy.

105. Mr. Black asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government if he will bring forward proposals for amending or repealing the provisions of the Town and Country Planning Act, 1947, dealing with the compulsory acquisition of development rights.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I would refer the hon. Member to my reply given yesterday to the hon. Member for Orkney and Shetland (Mr. J. Grimond).

106. Mr. Anthony Greenwood asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government what steps are taken to prevent vessels in the Port of London discharging black smoke in unreasonable quantities and so polluting the atmosphere.

Mr. H. Macmillan: The Port health authority is the Common Council of the City of London. Their inspectors, who 28 patrol the river, require the master of any ship which is discharging smoke too heavily to abate the nuisance. In exceptional cases the authority can take proceedings.
107. Mr. E. Wakefield asked the Minister of Works what has happened to the pelicans that used to inhabit the lake in St. James's Park.

Mr. Eccles: There were, until recently, two pelicans in St. James's Park. One of the birds, aged about 60, died on 13th October; he had been blind for some time, and was kept on Duck Island. The other, a much younger bird, died on 27th October, of lung disease. The right sort of birds are difficult to get but the Department is trying to replace these amiable inhabitants of St. James's Park. Meanwhile, the Zoological Society of London has kindly lent one.
108. Mr. Keeling asked the Minister of Works if he will make a statement about the future of the Festival of Britain buildings on the South Bank.

Mr. Eccles: Negotiations are proceeding with various interested bodies and I am not able to make a general statement. My Department is taking the lease of the greater part of the area between County Hall and Hungerford Bridge and it is probable that most of the buildings there will have to be removed. The future of the remainder of the Festival site will have to be considered by the London County Council and by my right hon. Friend the Minister of Housing and Local Government in the light of joint recommendations of the architect and the Chief Parks Officer of the Council and Mr. Hugh Casson, until recently Director of Architecture for the Festival of Britain.
111. Mr. Blenkinsop asked the Minister of Works whether he will take steps to ensure that all portable gas and electric fires are fitted with guards to help reduce their danger to children.

Mr. Eccles: Guards are included in the specifications for these fires recently published by the British Standards Institution. The Manufacturers' Associations have promised my Department to urge their members to observe the new specifications.
112. Mr. Chetwynd asked the Minister of Works whether he will reduce the amount of licence-free building work and thereby provide additional labour for the building of new houses.
Mr. Eccles: No. I do not consider that such a reduction would make any appreciable difference to the building of new houses or would justify the extra work on staff and burden on the public.

113. Mr. Slater asked the Minister of Works if he is aware that the Miners' Hostel, Dean Road, Ferryhill, County Durham, has been vacant for the last four weeks; and what is his intention in regard to this hostel.
Mr. Eccles: This hostel was given up by the National Coal Board on 5th October and has now been allocated for Government storage.
114. Mr. Watkinson asked the Minister of Labour if he will give the figures for unemployed workers and those on short time or part time at the latest convenient date.

Sir W. Monckton: At 15th October there were 263,756 unemployed persons on the registers of employment exchanges in Great Britain. The total number of workpeople on short-time is not known, but at establishments in manufacturing industries from which returns were received in respect of the week ended 22nd September the number on short-time in that week was 66,000. Estimates of the numbers of women normally working part-time, that is less than 30 hours a week, are available only for the manufacturing industries, the distributive and catering trades, laundries and cleaning and certain other services. The total number at 22nd September, 1951, for all these industries and services was 655,000.
116. Air Commodore Harvey asked the Minister of Labour the number of unemployed men and women in Macclesfield, Congleton and Bollington, respectively; and the number on short-time work.

Sir W. Monckton: At 15th October, 113 males and 175 females at Macclesfield, and 18 males and 141 females at Congleton. There is no employment exchange at Bollington, which is in the area of the Macclesfield Employment Exchange. As regards short-time work, I regret that statistics for local areas are not available.
117. Mr. Porter asked the Minister of Labour what steps he proposes to take to settle the difference between the Rugby League and the Players' Union.

118. Mr, J. P. W. Mallalieu asked the Minister of Labour whether he is prepared to set up an independent tribunal to inquire into the disagreement between the Rugby League Football Players' Union and Welfare Organisation and the Rugby League Council.

Sir W. Monckton: This dispute was formally reported by the Players' Union to my predecessor in July last, and since that time officers of my Department have been in close contact with representatives of the League and the Union with a view to promoting joint discussions between them. A joint meeting was held on 13th September last but, unfortunately, no progress could be made towards a settlement of the difficulties. Efforts have since been made to arrange a further joint meeting, but as it has not been found possible to reach an agreed basis for such a meeting, I have now decided to refer the dispute to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal in accordance with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Order No. 1376.
121. Mr. Baird asked the Minister of Labour the number of unemployed disabled persons in the Wolverhampton and Bilston area.
Sir W. Monckton: At 15th October, 49 at Wolverhampton and 8 at Bilston; including 16 and 4 respectively who are classified as unlikely to obtain employment other than under special conditions.

119. Mr. Watkins asked the Minister of Labour whether he is aware that notices of deferment of the call-up for agricultural workers do not state the procedure to be undertaken by employers to renew such deferment; and whether he will indicate what is the proper procedure under the recent arrangements.

Sir W. Monckton: Since the middle of October all notifications of the grant of deferment in respect of an agricultural worker have contained the following note: "If, when the current period of determent is nearing expiry, you consider that an extension of deferment is essential, you should apply on the prescribed form (N.S. 308) not later than seven days before the expiry date."
115. Mr. Mikardo asked the Minister of Labour when he expects to be able to report further progress on the establishment of a revised cost-of-living index.

Sir W. Monckton: The Cost of Living Advisory Committee is now considering a report submitted to them by the Technical Committee, which has been reviewing the operation of the Interim Index of Retail Prices since its introduction it. 1947 and has been considering possible means of effecting temporary modifications in the present index until a new index based on the results of a family budget enquiry can be instituted. I hope to receive a report on these matters from the Advisory Committee very shortly.

122. Mr. Emrys Hughes asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what is his estimate of the number of houses to be built in Scotland in 1952; and what are his proposals for increasing the number of building workers to be employed on municipal housing in Scotland.

Mr. J. Stuart: I hope that more houses will be built in Scotland in 1952 than in 1951, but I am not in a position to make a precise estimate. The labour force on local authority housing in Scotland is increasing and I shall do everything possible to continue this trend.

123. Major Anstruther-Gray asked the Secretary of State for Scotland whether his attention has been drawn to an experiment carried out by the Eastern Federation of Building Trades Employers at Ipswich in constructing houses with a high standard of amenity at low cost; and whether he will investigate how far this experiment can be usefully developed in Scotland.

Mr. J. Stuart: I am aware of the Ipswich experiment. I am sending my hon. and gallant Friend a copy of a circular with sketch plans which my Department issued to Scottish local authorities in August last on the subject of low cost housing.
124. Mr. Rankin asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what steps he is taking to deal with the shortage of accommodation in Glasgow for mentally defective children.
Mr. J. Stuart: The Regional Hospital Board are preparing plans for two projects, providing 350 additional beds serving the Glasgow area, and other proposals are at earlier stages of consideration.
Mr. H. Fraser asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how much land is farmed by his Department of Agriculture.
Mr. J. Stuart: The Department of Agriculture farm 131,917 acres of land, consisting in the main of hill farming subjects.

Mr. H. Fraser asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how much land is owned by his Department of Agriculture and, of this, how much is devoted to forestry, farming and smallholding use, respectively.

Mr. J. Stuart: 'The Secretary of State owns 508,057 acres of land under agricultural powers. Land settlement estates account for 456,569 acres and the remainder is held for farming use. Woodland areas extend to just over 2,000 acres. In addition, the Secretary of State owns 973,787 acres of land under forestry powers: of this land the Department of Agriculture at present factor or farm 263,419 acres. The remaining area,
33 which includes 289,331 acres actually under trees, is managed by the Forestry Commission.
Mr. Grimond asked the Secretary of State for Scotland when it is intended to announce the Royal Commission on self-government for Scotland.

Mr. J. Stuart: The Government will consider the terms of reference of a Royal Commission in the light of the report of the committee presided over by Lord Catto which is investigating the economic and financial relations between Scotland and the rest of the United Kingdom.
Mr. Emrys Hughes asked the Lord Advocate if he will consider an appeal in the case of the officials of the Knock- shinnoch colliery.
The Lord Advocate: Yes. A stated case has been applied for and is at present in course of adjustment.

125. Mr. Ellis Smith asked the Minister of Agriculture what steps it is proposed to take to deal with the serious flooding of houses in East Vale, Longton and Fenton: and if he will treat this matter as one of extreme urgency.

Mr. Nugent: I am informed that the Trent River Board and the Stoke-on-Trent Corporation are investigating this problem as a matter of urgency and I expect to receive a report within a few days. I will then write to the hon. Member.
Brigadier Clarke asked the Secretary of State for War (1) what complaints he has received regarding the messing on H.M.T. "Devonshire";
(2) if he will investigate and report on the conditions aboard H.M.T. "Devon- shire," on her recent voyage from Korea, in view of the complaints made.

Mr. Head: Some minor complaints about the messing, namely, that there were not enough green vegetables, the menus lacked variety and the tea was too weak, were made by a few of the men. So far as possible these shortcomings were rectified and, apart from these matters, the general standard of messing is reported to have been satisfactory. I do not propose to order any special inquiry into the conditions on this vessel, since it is already earmarked for conversion to post-war standards as soon as our present heavy movement commitments allow.

Miss Ward asked the Minister of Education if she will circulate in the OFFICIAL. REPORT details of the reduction in the number of new schools in the appropriate local education authority areas affected by the instructions issued prior to 25th October to cut their education estimates by 25 per cent.

Miss Horsbrugh: No instructions were issued by my Department to any local education authorities to cut their education estimates by 25 per cent. In compiling the 1952–53 building programme, which was announced about two months ago, and to which I think my hon. Friend must be referring, it was not possible to accept all the projects submitted by local education authorities. For England and Wales as a whole, however, the programme represents a total value of work rather greater than the programme for 1951–52.

Mr. Langford-Holt asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs if he is satisfied that the measures being taken in the Suez Canal zone are adequate to prevent disturbance of civil order and to protect British lives and property.

Mr. Nutting: I regret to inform the House that, with certain exceptions, so far from taking the necessary measures the Egyptian Government have connived in, if not encouraged, the spread of lawlessness in the Zone. In addition to their failure to take measures in time to pre
35 vent the incursion of hooligan elements which inspired the riots in Ismailia on 16th October, the Egyptian authorities have tolerated and even encouraged a widespread campaign of intimidation against Egyptian labour employed both in British military installations in the Canal ports and in private British employment. We have evidence of the direct participation of the local Egyptian authorities in this campaign and have been obliged to insist upon the expulsion of a number of minor officials involved, including a few police officers as well as members of terrorist organisations.

One of the effects of this Egyptian campaign has been to deprive a large part of the civil population of their means of livelihood. As a result of this and of the panic and departure of small shopkeepers, there is a danger that the whole system of food distribution, particularly in Ismailia and the villages of the Zone, will break down, leading to widespread distress and further disorder. At no time have His Majesty's Forces in any way interfered with the movement of food supplies into this area and the responsibility for this dangerous situation rests entirely on the shoulders of the Egyptian Government. So far, the Egyptian Government have shown no sign that they recognise the gravity of their responsibilities, and if their own people are to be spared from unnecessary hardship and suffering, urgent action is required on the part of the Egyptian authorities to put an end to this campaign of intimidation and restore normal conditions of life in the area.

Mr. Hylton-Foster asked the Minister of Health what steps have been taken to secure reciprocal facilities for British subjects while in Switzerland, having regard to the National Health Service facilities given to Swiss nationals who come to this country.
Mr. Crookshank: Inquiries have been made of the Swiss Government, but so far without success.

Mr. Hylton-Foster asked the Minister of Health if he will review the amount which a local authority is required to assume will be needed for their personal requirements by persons liable to pay for accommodation provided under Part III of the National Assistance Act, 1948, so that in appropriate cases such persons may benefit from the increased rates of retirement pensions now payable.

Mr. Crookshank: My hon. and learned Friend's suggestion would substantially increase the charges falling on public funds and it would not be right for me to hold out hope that this might be possible at the present time.
Mr. Hastings asked the Minister of National Insurance what is the annual sum paid to sufferers from tuberculosis through National Insurance benefit and National Assistance payments.
Mr. Peake: I regret that the information asked for is not available.

Brigadier Peto asked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he is aware that the number of firearms certificates for the purchase of automatic firearms by Egyptian nationals in this country needs attention, so as to minimise the number of firearms being exported from this country to Egypt; and what limitation is in force at present.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: Before granting a firearm certificate the chief officer of police concerned has to be satisfied that there is a good reason for doing so. I have no reason to think that, in exercising his power under the Firearms Act, any chief officer of police would facilitate the export of firearms to Egypt in present circumstances. I am informed that any Board of Trade licences for the export of arms to Egypt valid on 22nd October, 1951, were revoked on that date and that none has since been issued.

Captain Ryder asked the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he is aware that the awards for those disabled while serving in the police, prior to July, 1948, are considerably lower than the awards paid after that date under the Industrial Injuries Act; and whether he will take steps to remove this anomaly.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: I am aware that in some cases a policeman injured in the 38 execution of his duty before the Industrial Injuries Scheme came into operation might have received larger aggregate benefits if that scheme had applied to him. It is, however, the general practice for benefits introduced as from a specified date to be payable only to persons whose entitlement to benefit arises on or after that date, and I can find no grounds for suggesting that the police should receive exceptionally favourable treatment in this respect.
21.Mr. Shepherd asked the Assistant Postmaster General when the postal registration service started to show a loss; and what is the explanation.
Mr. Gammans: The registration service has shown a loss over the last 25 years: the fees charged have not covered rising costs.

44. Mr. J. Hynd asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs what steps the Government now proposes to take to obtain recovery of the compensation due to this country from Albania under the award of the International Court of Justice.

Mr. Nutting: His Majesty's Government are awaiting the decision of the arbitration, the arrangements for which were published in White Paper No. Cmd. 8242. The arbitrator has now been appointed and he called a meeting of the agents of the Governments concerned on the 5th of this month at Brussels. The meeting was attended by the agents of the United Kingdom, United States, French and Italian Governments and the arbitrator, after hearing the agents, gave decisions with regard to the procedure to be followed.

54. Mr. Alport asked the Minister of Food if he is aware of the serious consequences to United Kingdom apple growers arising from the present large scale imports of foreign apples; and what steps he intends to take to ensure that British growers have reasonable security in the home market.

Major Lloyd George: Imports of apples this season have so far been very small and should not have affected the sale of good quality home-grown apples. The recent reduction of food imports will cut down imports of Continental apples substantially. Home growers should have little difficulty in marketing the remainder of their crop.

56. Mr. Fenner Brockway asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies whether his attention has been drawn to the judgment given in the Nairobi courts in favour of ex-Chief Koinange, who had been prosecuted for growing coffee; and whether he will now proceed to abolish all discrimination between Africans and Europeans in relation to coffee growing.

Mr. Lyttelton: The answer to the first part of the Question is, "Yes." I do not accept the implication in the last part of the Question. Coffee growing by Europeans and by Africans is controlled in different ways because of differing needs. It is not a matter of discrimination but of facilitating the growth of coffee by the most suitable methods in each case.
61. Mr. Fenner Brockway asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies why meetings of the Kenya African Union in the Central Province, Kenya, have been prohibited.

Mr. Lyttelton: Meetings by the Kenya African Union in the Central Province of Kenya have been prohibited in three instances. In one case permission to hold a meeting was refused because it was intended to hold it on the football ground at a time when a match was due to be played. In two other instances the result of meetings held by the Union was such that it seemed likely that further meetings would lead to a breach of the peace. Meetings have, therefore, been temporarily prohibited in these two districts.
62. Mr. Fenner Brockway asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies why the age group meetings among the Kikuyu Tribe have been prohibited in Kenya.

Mr. Lyttelton: They have not been so prohibited. Certain Africans held age group meetings in 1950 to collect funds for the African Independent College at Githunguri. They applied again earlier this year to hold such meetings. They were asked to publish accounts showing
41 the collections made at their earlier meetings and how the money had been dispensed. This they have failed to do and they have made no further application to hold such meetings.

57. Mr. P. Roberts asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies whether he will take immediate steps to investigate the possibility of developing the iron ore resources of Sierra Leone, to overcome the shortages of this material which may handicap steel production in the future in this country.

Mr. Lyttelton: The company now working iron ore at Marampa is actively pursuing the possibility of developing further deposits. It will, however, take at least five years to bring in further production since a railway extension of about 80 miles will have to be built and the handling capacity of the port increased.

60. Mr. Thomas Reid asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies how it is proposed to finance the development plan approved by the Gold Coast Government costing about £75,000,000 and the Volta River Project costing about £105,000,000.

Mr. Lyttelton: The methods proposed for financing the Gold Coast Development Plan are set out in Chapter 6 of the Plan itself. I am sending a copy to the hon. Member. The Volta River project is still at the stage of discussion and I have no statement to make at present on how it would be financed.

64. Mr. Osborne asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies what was the purchase price of the s.s. "African Queen"; how much was spent on refitting and converting her; what was her operational cost; why she has been withdrawn; and what is the total estimated loss.

75. Captain Duncan asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies what was the cost of buying and equipping the s.s. "African Queen"; what revenue has been obtained from catching sharks 42 off West Africa; what is the total loss to the taxpayer to date; and if he will drop this venture.

Mr. Lyttelton: As already announced, the Colonial Development Corporation has abandoned this scheme. The total cost of the vessel and its conversion was £304,200. Operating and administration costs of the ship and shore station for the nine months from January to September, 1951, amounted to £134,827. The total revenue from all fishing, chiefly shark fishing, is expected to be about £18,000. The Corporation withdrew the ship because of the high cost of operation coupled with the severe fall in the price of vitamin A oil, the scheme's primary product. The Corporation cannot estimate the loss sustained until the assets are realised.
71. Mr. Sorensen asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies in view of the great hardship caused in Sierra Leone by the increasing cost of living, what action is being taken to meet this problem.

Mr. Lyttelton: It would be wrong to assume that the bulk of the population, namely, the farmers, who are receiving good prices for their produce, are suffering hardship in consequence of the rise in the cost of living. The effects of the rise are felt mainly by the wage-earning and urban communities. Substantial wage increases have been awarded to the lower paid workers during the last six months. The Sierra Leone Government is fully aware of the problem and the measures it is taking include control of the retail price of rice, purchase of stocks of rice for release when supplies are short, and various schemes for increased local production of staple foodstuffs.
72. Mr. Sorensen asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies the official results of the Nigerian elections including the support given to the respective parties.

Mr. Lyttelton: The elections are not complete and it would be premature to make a statement. Seventy-two seats out of 80 in the Western House of Assembly have been filled. The final election of members to the Northern and Eastern Houses of Assembly has yet to take place. I will provide the House with information on the results when the elections are finished.
58. Air Commodore Harvey asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies if he will make a statement regarding the death of the High Commissioner for Malaya, Sir Henry Gurney.

Mr. Lyttelton: The murder of Sir Henry Gurney by Communist terrorists was a grievous blow to all who uphold the cause of freedom in Malaya. Moving tributes have been paid to his memory not only by leaders of all the Malayan communities, but by people in all walks of life. I should like now to associate myself with these tributes and to express my sympathy with Lady Gurney and her sons. Sir Henry Gurney was an outstanding colonial servant who had devoted himself to the task of laying the foundations of a united Malayan nation and who died in the service of that cause.
I reaffirm the determination of His Majesty's Government to rid Malaya of terrorism.
59. Air Commodore Harvey asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies if he will make a statement on the present position in Malaya.

Mr. Lyttelton: The heavy casualties suffered by the security forces and civilians in October show the seriousness of the situation in Malaya. I can, however, report considerable progress in the resettlement of squatters and in the improvement of the intelligence organisation. The murder of Sir Henry Gurney has aroused the leading members of all communities to the need to strengthen the drive to rid the country of Communist terrorism. I should prefer to defer any further comment until after my return from Malaya.

69. Major Beamish asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies what regulations are in force in Malaya regarding the use of soft or armoured vehicles when senior officials are travelling by road in areas in which bandits are known to operate: and in what type of vehicle the late Sir Henry Gurney was travelling at the time that he was killed.

Mr. Lyttelton: The arrangements for the protection of senior officials while travelling by road in Malaya have now been revised and strengthened, but it would not be in the public interest to divulge particulars. At the time of his death Sir Henry Gurney was travelling in his official car, a Rolls Royce of standard design.

Mr. Janner asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies whether he will now circulate a full list of the names of rubber planters who have lost their lives in Malaya since the commencement of the emergency, including the dates on which they were killed and the compensation which has been granted in each case.
Mr. Lyttelton: I have not yet received the information but I have consulted the Acting High Commissioner and will write to the hon. Member when I have his reply.
63. Mr. R. Robinson asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies what steps have now been taken for the rehabilitation of Jamaica following the recent hurricane.

66. Mr. Smithers asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies whether he will make a statement with regard to the progress of relief and reconstruction measures in connection with the hurricane in Jamaica.

Mr. Lyttelton: Immediate relief was vigorously organised by the Governor; towards this His Majesty's Government contributed £250,000, for which a supplementary Vote will shortly be presented. Building materials to the value of £250,000 have already been distributed free. £45,000 worth of seed is being given to farmers. Within 10 days of the hurricane the Jamaica Government promised the banana industry £½million towards the cost of clearing and replanting and the work has gone ahead rapidly.

Subject to Parliamentary approval, His Majesty's Government will contribute up to a further £3,100,000 by grant and £1,500,000 by interest-free loan towards the cost of reconstruction. Detailed
45 schemes for using this money in restoring agriculture and in rehousing have recently been received from the Governor and are being considered urgently.

65. Mr. Smothers asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies whether he will make a statement with regard to the findings of the Commission which has made proposals for the future constitutional development of British Guiana.
Mr. Lyttelton: I have at present nothing to add to the despatch which my predecessor sent to the Governor and which was published with the report of the Commission last month.
73. Mr. R. Robinson asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies what steps are being taken to develop the rice industry in British Guiana.

Mr. Lyttelton: The Colony's consulting engineer is completing a comprehensive water control plan for the whole coastland. where rice is grown, and upwards of £750,000 has been allocated under the Colonial Development and Welfare Acts to enable a start to be made on the first stages of the plan. His Majesty's Government have undertaken to do their utmost to facilitate the raising of a loan on the London market when further finance is required. Plans for expanding the rice industry are under discussion with the Colonial Development Corporation. In the meantime, experimental work is being carried out on rice production and milling.
70. Mr. H. Hynd asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies what is now-the position in regard to alien groups in illegal occupation of British territory in the Falkland Island Dependencies.

Mr. Lyttelton: The latest available information is as follows:
(a) Three Chilean parties are established:
(i) Six men at Greenwich Island (S. Shetlands Group). 46
(ii) Six men at Cape Legoupil (N.W. tip of Graham Land).
(iii) An estimate of ten men at Paradise Harbour (W. coast of Graham Land), although they had not been established at the time of the last British visit.
(b) Four, and possibly five, Argentine parties are established:
(i) Eleven men at Laurie Island (South Orkney Group).
(ii) Ten men at Deception Island (South Shetland Group).
(ii) Four men at Paradise Harbour (see above).
(iv) An uncertain number in the Melchior Islands (Palmer Archipelago, off the west coast of Graham Land).
(v) A party of uncertain number may possibly be established (report not yet confirmed) at Marguerite Bay. (W. coast of Graham Land).
76. Mr. G. Thomas asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government whether he will make a statement concerning his proposal to review the Rent Restriction Acts.
Mr. Marples: Yes. The Government will consider this matter in due course.

Mr. Lewis asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government what arrangements will be made for tenants of council houses to purchase these dwellings; and what percentage of the 300,000 houses will be for sale and to let, respectively.
Mr. Macmillan: I would refer the hon. Member to the statement which I made on this subject on 13th November.

Mr. Peter Freeman asked the Minister of Fuel and Power the number of horses used below ground in coal mines at the end of June, 1951; and the number used below ground in the Durham and
47 Northern (N. and C.) Divisions, as well as in the other divisions, at the same date.
Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: The latest information available is as follows:

tr.td: NUMBER OF HORSES USED BELOW GROUND IN COAL MINES AT 30TH JUNE, 1950

body.p: Mr. Peter Freeman asked the Minister of Fuel and Power the average annual rate of reduction in the number of horses and ponies used in coal mines in each of the 10-year periods from 1920 to 1930, 1930 to 1940 and from 1940 to 1950; and the reasons for the reduction rate in the respective periods.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: The average annual rates of reduction in the number of horses and ponies used in coal mines in the 10-year periods ended 1930, 1940 and 1950 were 1,810, 1,880 and 1,250 respectively. These reductions reflect the increasing mechanisation of the mines.

Mr. Peter Freeman asked the Minister of Fuel and Power the percentage of the coal output of each division at the end of June, 1951, as well as the percentage of the total output in all coalfields, that was carried by mechanical conveyors at or near the coal face.
Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: The percentage of coal output mechanically conveyed at the coal face in 1950 was as follows:
Mr. Hylton-Foster asked the Minister of Health if, with a view to avoiding the burden of travel, especially for old people, he will set up a distribution centre for hearing aids in York.
Mr. Crookshank: I very much regret that, both for financial and for other reasons, it is not possible for me to do this yet.

Mr. Peter Freeman asked the Minister of Food how many cattle and cows were killed for food in 1950; how many were inspected; how many were totally condemned as unfit for human consumption, and for what reason; and how many car-cases there were of which some part or organ was condemned and the percentage, in each case.
Major Lloyd George: The total numbers slaughtered for sale for human food in Great Britain in 1950 and the numbers wholly condemned after slaughter were as follow:

All animals slaughtered on behalf of my Department may be inspected by the meat inspectors of the local authorities. Where animals are accepted for slaughter as casualties or on the basis of owner's risk it is a condition of purchase that the carcass shall be examined by the meat inspector as the payment to the producer is based on the weight of the carcass, or part of the carcass, passed fit for human consumption. 117,145 cows and 189,884 other cattle were accepted under the latter arrangements and of these 20,556 cows and 6,110 other cattle were totally condemned and are included in the totals given above.

Records are not yet available from all local authorities of the number of carcasses of which parts only were condemned but we have records of the total weight of all condemned meat, including parts of carcasses, and the percentage which this bears
49 to the total weight of meat produced on slaughter during this period was as follow:
Records are not yet available from all the local authorities of the total number of carcasses examined by their meat inspectors or of the reasons for condemnation.
Mr. Black asked the Minister of Food how present meat consumption per head in this country compares with pre-war.

Major Lloyd George: The consumption of meat (including bacon) in terms of edible weight was 82.2 lb. per head of the civilian population in the 12 months ended June, 1951, compared with an average of 109.6 lb. before the war.

18.Mr. Rentonasked the Minister of Health what progress has been achieved by the Committee, appointed by his predecessor, to examine the need for the registration of opticians; and whether he will make a statement.
Mr. Crookshank: I understand that the Committee have finished taking evidence and hope to present their report early next year.

26.Mr. Hastingsasked the Minister of Health whether he has now initiated discussions with the chiropodists and other professions dealt with by the Cope Committees; and whether the memorandum which his Department proposed to send to the professional bodies concerned has yet been despatched.
Mr. Crookshank: Discussions with the professional bodies concerned have not yet started, but I will send them a memorandum as a basis for discussion during the next few weeks.
33.Mr. Shepherdasked the Minister of Labour the percentage of days lost through strikes in private and nationalised industries, respectively.

Sir W. Monckton: As all the industries concerned were not nationalised on the same date the information asked for by my hon. Friend is not readily available for earlier years. During the period 1st January, 1950, to 30th September last, about 35 per cent. of the number of working days lost in stoppages of work through industrial disputes was lost in industries which have been nationalised since 1945, and about 65 per cent. in other industries.
37.Mr. F. Andersonasked the Minister of Labour when buildings operations will commence for the new disabled persons factory at Cleator Moor, Cumberland.
Sir W. Monckton: I understand from Remploy Limited that plans for the new factory have been drawn up and that permits for buildings are now awaited.

Mr. Swinglerasked the Minister of Labour how many unfilled vacancies there are, at the latest date for which figures are available in the Royal Ordnance factories in the counties of Staffordshire and Cheshire; and how many in the coalmining industry in the same area.

Sir W. Monckton: At the beginning of November there were on the books of the employment exchanges approximately 600 unfilled vacancies in the Royal Ordnance Factories and 2,000 in the coalfields in the two counties.
Mr. J. E. Crowderasked the Minister of Labour what steps he is taking to provide an effective employment service for older people who are now having difficulty in getting work.

Sir W. Monckton: All employment exchanges have been instructed to give special help to older people who register for employment and to bring them to the attention of employers when they are suitable for the work.
Mr. Mellishasked the Minister of Labour what action he proposes to take on the recent White Paper concerning the London Docks.
Sir W. Monckton: I am at present studying the Report of the Leggett Committee.

43.Mr. Watkinsasked the Minister of Education what distance pupils in the primary schools in Radnorshire are expected to walk to school; how many prosecutions have taken place during the last 12 months against parents for not sending their children to school; and how
53 many children there are who have not yet attended school because of the lack of suitable transport arrangements.

Mr. Pickthorn: The normal walking distance for pupils in the primary schools of Radnorshire is two miles for those under eight years of age and three miles for those over eight years of age. During the last 12 months there have been 10 prosecutions against parents for not sending their children to school. There are, I understand, three children who have not yet attended school because of the lack of suitable transport arrangements.

44.Mr. Watkinsasked the Minister of Education what were the circumstances in which Mr. A. Bowkett, Cwm Farm, Pains-castle, Radnorshire, was prosecuted twice for not sending his children to school; how many times the school attendance officer visited the parents before the first prosecution took place; and whether the Education Committee of Radnor drew the attention of the Radnor Highways Committee to the bad state of the roads on which the children are expected to travel.

Mr. Pickthorn: The local education authority have a duty to institute proceedings wherever, in their opinion, it is necessary for the purpose of enforcing school attendance. The authority's action in this case was taken in the exercise of that duty: the school attendance officer visited the home on one occasion before the first prosecution; and the education committee did not specifically draw the attention of the highways committee to the state of any roads affecting the case.
77.Mr. Maudeasked the Minister of Education what steps she proposes to take to assist the voluntary schools, particularly in respect of the problem of displaced pupils.

Mr. Pickthorn: My right hon. Friend is considering the question of extending, within the framework of the Education Acts, the assistance at present available to voluntary schools; but she will not be in a position to make any statement until this matter has been considered in the light of all the circumstances and after discussion with the various interested parties.
78.Mr. Chetwyndasked the Minister of Education what cuts are planned in the school building programme.
80.Mr. Peartasked the Minister of Education what restrictions are to be placed on new school building.

Mr. Pickthorn: Until the Government have completed the review of capital expenditure in 1952, which was announced by my right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer on 7th November, no decision will be taken to alter the educational building programme.
82.Mrs. Corbetasked the Minister of Education what effect the decision not to grant new starting dates within the next three months will have on the building of schools urgently needed in London.

Mr. Pickthorn: It is impossible at this stage to assess the effect on the London school building programme of the decision to which the hon. Member refers. If the Government's object of relieving the overloading of the building industry is achieved, schools already started and those whose starting dates are delayed may be brought into use earlier than would otherwise have been possible.

79.Mr. Chetwyndasked the Minister of Education, in view of the proposed restrictions on new buildings whether she will give an assurance that the school meals service will be maintained at its present level.
Mr. Pickthorn: Yes.
81.Mr. Jannerasked the Minister of Education her plans for increasing the number of school dentists.
Mr. Pickthorn: My right hon. Friend hopes that the salary scales fixed earlier this year by the Dental Whitley Council will attract more dentists to the school dental service.
Mr. Swinglerasked the Minister of Education whether she will bring forward legislation to increase financial grants to church schools.
Mr. Pickthorn: I would refer the hon. Member to the answer given today to my hon. Friend the Member for Ealing, South (Mr. Maude).
51.Sir W. Smithersasked the Minister of Agriculture the profit or loss on farms run by county agricultural executive committees since the end of the war.

Sir T. Dugdale: It was not possible to prepare full trading accounts for county agricultural executive committees before the financial year 1948–49. The accounts of the committees for the financial years 1948–49 and 1949–50 appeared in the annual volumes of Trading Accounts and Balance Sheets for those years and disclosed losses on farming operations of£909,913 and£680,322, respectively. The volume for 1950–51 has not yet been published, but the accounts forwarded to the Comptroller and Auditor-General disclosed farming losses of£197,761. These losses were arrived at after charging overheads, including depreciation. administration and interest on capital.

52.Mr. Rentonasked the Minister of Agriculture how many acres of land in Huntingdonshire are considered by the county agricultural executive committee to be unnecessarily prevented from being cultivated owing to the presence of derelict aerodrome and hutted camp foundations and structures, etc.; and what steps are being taken to bring such land into production.

Sir T. Dugdale: I am informed that in Huntingdonshire about 1,200 acres of agricultural land are sterilised by concrete runways hut bases and other structures associated with airfields and military camps. To remove these obstructions would cost far more than would be justified by the gain in food production.
54.Mr. Lambertasked the Minister of Agriculture whether he will hold a supplementary price review this autumn; and if he will make a statement.
Sir T. Dugdale: I would refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave today to the hon. Member for Newbury (Mr. Hurd).
63.Mr. Hurdasked the Minister of Agriculture to what extent the output of British agriculture declined in the first nine months of 1951 compared with the previous year.

Sir T. Dugdale: There has been some reduction this year in the output of milk and eggs, but meat output has been maintained. Among crops, the production of wheat and oats this year is appreciably less than that of last year, but there was a somewhat heavier production of barley and mixed corn. Production of potatoes and sugar beet are both lower than last year. The fruit crop, particularly that of apples, has been heavier than in 1950.

Mr. Peter Freemanasked the Minister of Agriculture if he will introduce legislation to prevent accidents arising from the faulty use of electric milking apparatus; how many cases have been reported to him; and what steps are being taken to prevent any recurrence.

Sir T. Dugdale: I understand that a few cases of cows having been electrocuted in byres in recent years have been reported. Under Regulations, electricity boards require any installation to comply with certain safety standards, and I am not satisfied that further safety provisions are needed.

66.Mr. Hylton-Fosterasked the Minister of Agriculture if his attention has been called to the discomfort and inconvenience caused to many citizens of York by the flooding of the River Ouse; if he will consider with all the authorities concerned what can be done to prevent or reduce the risk of a recurrence; and in particular if he will consult with the Forestry Commission as to the possibility of improving the position by further afforestation.

Sir T. Dugdale: I am advised by the Yorkshire Ouse River Board, which is the responsible land drainage authority, that the recent flooding in York resulted
57 from an abnormally heavy and continuous rainfall in the two weeks ending 11th November, which caused the river to rise some 14 feet above its normal summer level.
