My Department will consider with the River Board whether remedial works to alleviate this flooding are practicable. Afforestation on such a scale as would have any significant effect on the run off into the River Ouse and its tributaries would not seem to offer a practical solution.
68.Mr. Swinglerasked the Chancellor of the Exchequer in what ways he proposes to recast the existing system of taxation on industrial and commercial profits.
Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: These are matters which will come under review in connection with the Budget, and I must ask the hon. Member to await my right hon. Friend's Budget statement.

69.Mr. J. Hyndasked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether he is aware of the difficulties caused to schools through the effect of Purchase Tax on school exercise books, pencils, drawing paper and other necessities; and what steps he proposes to take to relieve these difficulties.

Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: I appreciate that Purchase Tax does have the effect of increasing the cost of stationery and some other articles used in schools. It is, however, a general principle that Purchase Tax is charged irrespective of the use to which the taxable article will ultimately be put. Even if it were practicable to exempt articles bought for use in schools, this departure from principle could hardly be made in isolation from other cases which could be claimed to deserve special consideration, and it would be impossible to set a justifiable limit to such exceptions.

72.Mr. J. Hyndasked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether his attention has been drawn to the disabilities suffered 58 by co-operative societies due to the existing restrictions on the total individual shareholding of members; and whether he will introduce early legislation to bring the present limitation more into line with current values.
Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: The important issues raised in this Question are now being carefully considered, but I am afraid that I am not today in a position to make a statement.

75.Sir H. Williamsasked the Secretary to the Treasury the total value, c.i.f., of the imports of tobacco, wines, spirits and petroleum products on which Customs Duties were levied; and the total of such Customs Duties for 12 months ended 31st March, 1951.
Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: The figures for values c.i.f. and Customs Duty payments in respect of tobacco, wines, spirits and petroleum products for the year ended 31st March. 1951, are as follows:

tr.td: Total duty paid on clearances for home consumption*

* The duty figures relate to clearances for home consumption during the year in question, and not to goods actually imported during that year. For the most part, these goods are not duty paid at time of importation but subsequently when cleared for home consumption. As regards hydrocarbon oils there is the further point that the duty on refined oils (excluding most of the heavy oils) is chargeable on such oils produced in this country from imported crude

body.p: 74.Mr. Finlayasked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether lie will grant facilities for duty-free parcels to be sent by men on active service in Korea.

Mr. Boyd-Carpenter: The men on active service in Korea, in common with all troops serving abroad, are allowed to send home presents other than tobacco,
59 scent and liquor to the value of 10s. free of customs charges. Gift food parcels weighing not more than 22 lb. are also admitted duty free.

84.Mr. J. Johnsonasked the Under-Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations whether he will consider the establishment of executive and legislative councils in the High Commission Territories of Basutoland, Bechuanaland and Swaziland.

Mr. J. Foster: His Majesty's Government's aim is to develop representative and responsible institutions in the High Commission Territories. At their present stage of development the main emphasis is on local government. But all three Territories have advisory councils with territory-wide representation, which are consulted by the Resident Commissioners on important matters of concern to the inhabitants. Until further progress has been made, it would be premature to consider the grant of executive and legislative powers.

85.Mr. J. Johnsonasked the Under-Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations if he will consider the need of appointing a Royal Commission to inquire into the constitutional and economic conditions of the High Commission Territories of Basutoland, Bechuanaland and Swaziland.
Mr. J. Foster: No.

86.Mr. Sorensenasked the Under-Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations if he can make a statement in respect of the Bamangwato chieftainship; what developments have taken place; and what is now the policy of His Majesty's Government.

Mr. J. Foster: My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State is carefully studying the complicated problem which Bamangwato affairs present. Until he has made himself conversant with it, I can make no statement on his behalf.

87.Sir H. Williamsasked the Under-Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations if he will arrange to issue a White Paper on the subject of the visit to this country of the Paramount Chieftainess of the Basutos.

88.Mr. Hector Hughesasked the Under-Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations what subjects were discussed during the visit of the recent delegation from the Government of Basutoland to the British Government; and what was the result of the visit.

Mr. J. Foster: His Majesty's Government do not feel a White Paper is called for. The Paramount Chieftainess of Basutoland, accompanied by 11 of her principal chiefs and advisers, spent a month in this country. His Majesty's Government arranged for the party to see as much as possible of life and work in this country, especially agriculture, water storage, power production and local government, which are all relevant to Basutoland's progress. During their visit, the Basuto delivered a loyal address to His Majesty the King which contained a prayer for continued protection.

At a meeting with my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State, a number of problems affecting the administration and development of Basutoland were discussed. These included financial assistance, local government, the Jones Report on Medicine Murders, the system of Legal Appeals, Basutoland imports and mechanised Agriculture. The Basuto asked the Secretary of State for an assurance that the administration of their Territory would not be transferred to the Union of South Africa without their consent. In reply, my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State reiterated the pledges given by His Majesty's Government during the passage of the South Africa Bill through this House in 1909, and since repeated frequently by spokesmen of various United Kingdom Governments, namely, that no transfer should take place until the inhabitants of the Territory have been consulted and until this House has been given opportunity to express its views.

The Paramount Chieftainess has expressed her thanks to His Majesty's Goverment for the facilities and courtesies
61 afforded during the visit and she and her party returned home with an enthusiastic desire to apply to their own problems the knowledge gained from their visit.
I will gladly supply any additional information about the Basutos' visit and discussions here which the hon. Members may want if they will ask me for details.

89.Mr. Hector Hughesasked the Under-Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations if he has yet received a report from the three investigators who were sent by his predecessor to Bechuanaland; and when will their report be available.

Mr. J. Foster: Yes. The three observers who were sent to the Bamangwato Reserve to report on the attitude of the tribe to the question of Tshekedi Khama's return presented their reports in September to the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations. My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State is at present studying these and other reports on Bamangwato affairs, and I am not yet in a position to answer the last part of the Question.
Mr. Pagetasked the Under-Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations whether Mr. Tshekedi Khama has yet been granted permission to return to the house of his fathers.
Mr. J. Foster: No.
90.Mr. Jannerasked the President of the Board of Trade whether it is now proposed to introduce legislation dealing with the points covered by the Committee on Weights and Measures.
Mr. P. Thorneycroft: I am studying the Committee's Report and will make a statement later on the question of possible legislation.

94.Dr. Kingasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he will propose an amendment to the law concerning cruelty to children so as 62 to increase the maximum punishment for parents found guilty of neglecting their children or of treating them cruelly.

99.Mr. Hastingsasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether his attention has been called to the many cases of cruelty to children in their own homes that have occurred recently; and what steps he is taking to secure early notification so that preventive action may be taken before irrevocable damage has occurred.

104.Sir H. Roperasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he will institute an inquiry as to whether the law needs strengthening in relation to the prevention of offences of cruelty to children and to the punishment of such offences.

Colonel Stoddart-Scottasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department if, in view of the inadequate penalties recently imposed in cases of vicious cruelty to children, he will review the maximum penalties that can be imposed in the different courts, with a view to legislative action.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: Although the public conscience has been shocked by reports of certain serious cases, there is no evidence that there has been any marked increase of offences of ill-treatment or neglect of children, or that the maximum penalties provided are inadequate. Most offenders are dealt with in magistrates' courts, who can impose a sentence of up to six months' imprisonment.

But on conviction on indictment an offender may be sentenced to up to two years' imprisonment; and it is for those responsible for instituting prosecutions to consider in any particular case whether they should, instead of applying to the magistrates' court for summary trial, invite the justices to consider the question of committing for trial. It is also for the prosecuting authority to consider in cases where injuries are deliberately inflicted whether a charge should not be brought under the Offences against the Person Act, 1861, which provides even more severe penalties.

I do not think that there is occasion for a committee of inquiry or for amendment of the law. On the question of prevention, the measures taken to coordinate the efforts of statutory and voluntary services concerned with the welfare
63 of children neglected in their own homes were described in Chapter III of the Sixth Report of the Work of the Children's Department of the Home Office published last May.

95.Mr. Mikardoasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department what representations he has received from the National Association of Retired Police Officers concerning the level of police pensions; and whether he will make a statement.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: I have received no representations from this Association, but I have carefully reviewed the representations which were made to my predecessor. These were to the effect that police pensions should be re-assessed in the light of the prevailing cost of living and that pensions granted to police widows whose husbands died before 5th April, 1949, should be increased to the new rates introduced with effect from 1st July, 1949, in accordance with the recommendations of Lord Oaksey's Committee on Police Conditions of Service (Cmd. 7674). The first proposal affects all classes of public pensioners, and I would not feel justified in suggesting exceptional treatment in this matter for police pensioners.

As regards the second proposal, amendments to a pensions scheme are normally introduced as from a specified date, and I regret I cannot see my way to propose any alteration of the provisions of the Police Pensions Regulations in this respect.

105.Mr. Slaterasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he is aware that the wife of a retired police officer who marries him during the course of his retirement does not qualify for pension at his decease; and what steps he is taking to provide for such cases.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: This point was fully considered by the Oaksey Committee on Police Conditions of Service, who reached the conclusion that the considerations which justify special provison for the widows of police officers do not apply where the marriage takes place after the husband has retired. I agree with the Committee's conclusion.
96.Mr. Bennasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department approximately how many postal votes were cast at the recent General Election; or, alternatively, when the figures will be published.
Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: I have not yet received figures from all the returning officers. I will publish a summary as soon as they are available.

98.Mr. G. Thomasasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he is aware of the large number of electors in Ely, Cardiff, who were disfranchised at the General Election by the name of their street being left off the register; and whether he will institute an inquiry into this matter.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: This is the responsibility of the electoral registration officer, and I have no power to take any action. I have, however, been in communication with the electoral registration officer, who Worms me that a number of newly constructed houses in this street were unfortunately overlooked in the process of the house to house canvass. This omission was also not observed by the electors themselves or by the party agents when the lists were published for claims and objections to be made.

97.Mr. P. Robertsasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he will now give instructions that men in the fire service shall be treated for payment purposes on the same level as the police.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: Section 17 of the Fire Services Act, 1947, provides that the Secretary of State may make Regulations, inter alia, as to the pay and allowances of persons employed as members of fire brigades maintained by local authorities.

A National Joint Council for local authorities' fire brigades has been set up in England and Wales to consider questions arising as to the conditions of service of persons employed as members of
65 such brigades. The Secretary of State has recognised this Council as the proper body for the consideration of such questions, and in pursuance of the Act he is accordingly obliged to consult the Council before making any Regulations.

The constitution of the Council provides that in the event of any disagreement between the employers' side and the employees' side the matter in dispute shall, at the request of either side, be referred to the Minister of Labour and National Service for submission to one of the forms of arbitration provided by the Industrial Courts Act, 1919.

The National Joint Council has recently had under consideration a claim submitted by the employees' side for increased rates of pay. I am informed that the two sides have unhappily failed to reach agreement on the claim and that the matter in dispute has been reported to the Minister of Labour and National Service.
In the circumstances the question of action on my part does not arise.

100.Mrs. Whiteasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department what steps are being taken to investigate the financial relationship between England and Wales, on the lines of the Catto Committee investigation into Scottish finances.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: When the Government have received and considered the Report of the Committee referred to they will consider whether it would be advantageous for a similar investigation to take place as regards Wales.
102.Rev. LI. Williamsasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many members of the Welsh Advisory Council represent Monmouthshire.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: Individual local authorities are not represented as such on the Council. It so happens that there is at present no representative of Monmouthshire among the local authority representatives on the Council, but two other members of the Council have close associations with Monmouthshire.
106.Mr. G. Thomasasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department what policy he proposes to adopt in connection with the Welsh Advisory Council.
108.Mrs. Whiteasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department in what respects he contemplates changes in the status, constitution or programme of work of the Council for Wales.
Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: I regret that I am not yet in a position to make any statement on this subject, but it must not be assumed that any fundamental changes are contemplated.

101.Mr. Gibsonasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he will introduce legislation to prevent landlords and their agents interfering with the freedom of tenants of small houses using them as committee rooms during general or local elections.
Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: No.

107.Lieut.-Colonel Liptonasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he is satisfied that Thomas Kavanagh, aged 15 months, was taken from this country on 6th November with his parents' consent and if he will investigate this matter.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: It is the duty of the police to investigate when they have reason to suspect that a criminal offence may have been committed. The Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis informs me that this child's parents both state that they consented to his journey to America for a holiday of three months at the end of which time a further decision would be taken about the boy's future.
103.Rev. LI. Williamsasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department what steps he is taking to deal more drastically with persons convicted of driving vehicles under the influence of drink

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: I have no powers in this matter. It is entirely for the courts, on the evidence of all the circumstances, to assess what is the appropriate penalty in any particular case, and it would not be proper for me to offer them guidance in this matter. The maximum penalties prescribed by law are heavy, and the courts, have an ample reserve of power to deal with the most serious cases. The Lord Chief Justice, in a recent case before the Divisional Court, took the opportunity of calling the attention of magistrates to the fact that driving under the influence of drink was one of the worst offences which it was possible to commit and I have no doubt that courts will pay proper attention to this advice.
109.Mr. Haleasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he is now in a position to make a statement of the Government's intentions on the question of electoral reform.
Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: I have nothing to add to the statement made by my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister in the debate on the Address on 6th November.

111.Mr. Jannerasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he is aware that there are at present no approved schools for epileptic children and that disposal in such cases by the juvenile courts is therefore difficult; and whether he will take steps to make accommodation available for delinquent epileptic children.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: Approved schools deal with a number of children and young persons suffering from minor epilepsy, but the schools are not designed to give the specialist and long-term medical treatment required by the few persons suffering from major epilepsy who are sent to approved schools. I am in consultation with my right hon. Friends the Minister of Health and the Minister of Education about the question of the appropriate provision to be made for these cases.
112.Mr. H. Hyndasked the Secretary of State for the Home Department when the remand and detention centres envisaged by the Criminal Justice Act, 1948, will be provided.

Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: Owing to the restrictions on capital investment it is not possible to provide new building in the immediate future for the purpose of remand and detention centres. Remand centres require new building, and in present circumstances no progress with them can be made. The Prison Commissioners are, however, proposing to set up one or two experimental detention centres in adapted premises and it is hoped that the first may be ready for occupation next spring.

113.Mr. Hector Hughesasked the Secretary of State for Scotland what were the rates of infant and maternal mortality in Scotland for each of the five years, respectively, preceding and succeeding the Second World War; and what were the causes of these differences.
Mr. J. Stuart: The infant mortality and maternal mortality for the years 1934–38, and 1946–50, are as follows:

Many factors have contributed to the general improvement, including better living conditions flowing from a generally higher level of employment, better standards of maternal care, and the treatment of infections by new drugs including the antibiotics. It is not possible to set down in order of importance specific
69 causes for the general improvement, but it may be accepted that deaths from diarrhoeal diseases and respiratory infections contributed largely to the set-backs in infant mortality in 1936–37, and 1947.

115.Mr. Awberyasked the Minister of Transport if he is aware that a 10 per cent. reduction on the maintenance of roads in Bristol recently made by him will reduce the standard of public safety on the roads as well as affect the efficiency of the vehicles using them; and if he will now withdraw his requirement to cut this expenditure.

Mr. Maclay: I assume that the hon. Member is referring to Circular No. 672 issued to local highway authorities on the 26th October last asking them to limit their expenditure on unclassified roads in the remainder of the current financial year to 90 per cent. of the unspent balance of the provision made in their budget for 1951–52 and asking them to budget for an expenditure on unclassified roads in 1952–53 not exceeding 90 per cent. of their estimate for the current year. This was a request, not a formal requirement, but in view of the need for strict limitation of capital expenditure I hope that local highway authorities will comply with it, subject to any further guidance that may be given them when the Government have been able to review the position in more detail.

116.Mr. Vaughan-Morganasked the Minister of National Insurance how far the recent alterations to retirement pension increments have been successful in inducing men over 65 and women over 60 to remain at work; and if he will publish the relevant statistics.

Mr. Turton: It is too early to have any reliable information on this point. It will in any case always be difficult to isolate the effects of a particular provision which is only one factor among several influencing a person who is considering whether to stay on at work or to claim retirement pension.

117.Mr. Awberyasked the Minister of Works if, in applying the restriction on building work for the next three months, he will arrange for those towns that were heavily damaged in the war to receive some priority for their re-building in order that they may restore business to normal as quickly as possible.

Mr. Eccles: No. On taking office the Government found that more buildings had been started than could be economically completed with the labour and materials available. Accordingly the temporary restriction on fresh building work was imposed in the general interest so that this over-loading could quickly be corrected and better progress made on work already in hand. It is, therefore, in the interests of the war-damaged towns that we should make this period as short as possible by allowing exceptions only for cases of extreme urgency.

Mr. E. Wakefieldasked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs the cost, for the year 1950–51, of the establishment maintained by his Department at Bahrein; and what were the comparable figures for the year 1946–47.

Mr. Nutting: The net cost to the Foreign Service Vote of maintaining the establishment at Bahrein for the year 1950–51 was approximately£54,500. The comparable figure for 1946–47 when the post was maintained by the Government of India was approximately£56,500.

Mr. Doddsasked the Chancellor of the Exchequer to what extent he proposes to cut building construction work other than housing; and what priority is to be given to factories, schools, public amenities and renovations or readjustments of older buildings.
Mr. R. A. Butler: Decisions on these matters will emerge from the review of the building programme which, as I informed the House in my speech on 7th November, is being undertaken.

Mrs. Mannasked the Minister of Food if he is satisfied that the supply of national full cream dried milk will remain available for babies: and if this will be of the same quality and quantity and at the same price as at present.

Major Lloyd George: We certainly intend to maintain the quality and quantity of national dried milk which we regard as an important part of the welfare foods service. I cannot, of course, promise that there will never be any change in the price but we have no present intention of altering it.
Mr. Hastingsasked the Minister of Health what is the annual cost of treatment of tuberculosis in hospitals and sanatoria, and in the home.

Mr. Crookshank: I regret that this information is not available. Much tuberculosis treatment is comprised within the work of general hospitals and it would be hard to separate its cost. Nor is it practicable to keep separate account of how much of the cost of the general practitioner service is attributable to domiciliary treatment of tuberculosis patients.

Mr. Burdenasked the Minister of Health if, in view of the delay which now ensues between the prescribing of a deaf aid to be supplied under the National Health Service and the actual provision of the aid, he will issue a direction to hospital authorities that patients shall be told how long it will be before they receive their deaf aid, thus giving them an opportunity if they so desire to purchase this privately.
Mr. Crookshank: I regret the delay that still continues but I do not think this is a matter calling for any general direction by me.
Mr. Errollasked the Minister of Health what discussions have been started with the professions covered by the Cope Committee on Medical Auxiliaries.
Mr. Crookshank: I would refer my hon. Friend to the reply given today to the hon. Member for Barking (Mr. Hastings).
Mr. G. Thomasasked the Minister of Health the date on which construction will begin on the new training hospital at Cardiff.
Mr. Crookshank: I cannot yet say when building will begin, as the stage of preliminary planning has not yet been completed.

Mr. Peter Freemanasked the Minister of Fuel and Power the number of small 10-ton locomotives now used below grounds in mines; and what encouragement of the use of electric battery and diesel locomotives of this and smaller weight for haulage in mines at or near the coal face has been officially given by his Department.

Mr. Geoffrey Lloyd: latest available figures relate to 31st December, 1950, when there were 313 locomotives of 12 tons weight or less used below ground in coal mines. The reply to the second part of the Question is that the installation of locomotives in coal mines is not a matter for my Department but for the N.C.B., who must have regard to the lay-out of the mines, the size and gradients of the roads, the safety with which they can be used, and other factors.
Squadron Leader Cooper asked the Minister of Education if she will give the number of school dental officers employed by local authorities per month from January 1951 to the most convenient date.

Mr. Pickthorn: The latest figures available are those showing the position at the beginning of last January, when the number of dentists in the school dental service was equivalent to 717 full-time officers. Figures showing the present position are being collected and my right hon. Friend will send them to my hon. and gallant Friend as soon as she has them.
Mr. Grimond asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will increase the grants available under the Housing Acts for the improvement of housing by private owners.
Mr. Stuart: I am not yet in a position to make a statement on this subject.
Mr. de Freitas asked the Under-Secretary of State for Air how many houses were completed on Royal Air Force stations in Lincolnshire in 1949 and 1950 and the first 10 months of 1951.
Mr. Birch: The numbers for permanent married quarters are 156, 203 and 171 respectively

Mr. Swingler asked the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he has considered the renewed application of the borough council of Newcastle-under-Lyme for the same functions in Civil Defence as have already been conferred on the borough councils of Cambridge, Chesterfield, Luton and Swindon: and if he will now amend the appropriate regulations so as to include Newcastle-under-Lyme.
Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe: The application is being considered, and I hope to 74 let the borough council of Newcastle-under-Lyme have my decision very soon.

Sir W. Smithers asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer, to the nearest £1 million, the amount of debt held by Government Departments on 31st March, 1951, under the separate heading of floating debt, other internal debt, excluding bonds tendered for Death Duties, and Treasury guaranteed securities, together with the names of the principal Government Departments including in the compilation.
Mr. R. A. Butler: I would refer my hon. Friend to page 7 of the latest National Debt Return (Cmd. 8384). I regret that I cannot add to the published information.

Mr. MacColl asked the Minister of Housing and Local Government how many local authorities of each type have obtained exemption from submitting house plans to his Department by certifying that they have been prepared by a qualified architect and how many houses are covered by such certificates.
Mr. H. Macmillan: I regret that this information is not readily available and could not be given without considerable research.

Sir H. Webbe asked the President of the Board of Trade if he will introduce legislation to implement the recommendation on page 99 of the Report of the Committee on Weights and Measures Legislation, Command Paper No. 8219. relating to the standardisation of the size of bottles containing alcoholic liquor, and, in particular, to the legalisation of the denominations of ⅔pint and⅔quart being the normal quantities in which spirits are bottled.
Mr. P. Thorneycroft: I would refer my hon. Friend to the reply I gave yesterday to the hon. Member for Leicester, North-West (Mr. Janner).
